items.summary: Audited research compendium supporting the evaluation of Big Five league representation as a candidate squad-composition performance indicator for FIFA World Cup knockout progression from 1998 to 2026. The release contains 1,584 first-knockout starting-eleven records nested within 144 team-tournaments across eight men’s World Cups and 48 national teams. The analytical framework evaluates three linked properties: discrimination between levels of format-harmonised knockout progression; incremental information beyond pre-tournament World Football Elo; and transportability of any increment to World Cup editions and national teams excluded from model estimation. The 1998–2010 historical extension preserves the frozen exposure, outcome and model definitions established for 2014–2026. Historical starter status derives from the Fjelstul World Cup Database and was cross-checked against RSSSF match details. Club affiliation and top-division status were adjudicated using tournament squad records and season-specific domestic-league reference files. The 2014–2026 subset retains the completed provenance audit, including 505 re-checked starter records, 13 starter-name corrections, 45 club-affiliation checks and seven Big Five reclassifications. Analyses include tournament-adjusted ordinal and cut-point models, AICc comparison with Akaike weights, 5,000 national-team cluster-bootstrap samples with bias-corrected and accelerated intervals, leave-one-edition-out validation, leave-one-national-team-out validation, a strict 2026 temporal and tournament-format holdout, and a predictive cluster bootstrap that refits both competing models within every fold and resample. Additional checks address collinearity, edition adjustment and dependence through within-edition permutation testing and an edition-level block bootstrap. Big Five representation was associated with deeper knockout progression before adjustment for Elo, but this association attenuated after adjustment. Model comparisons and held-out evaluations did not establish a stable, transportable increment beyond prior team strength. These findings concern the predictive information provided by current league representation; they do not distinguish the mechanisms through which players enter elite leagues or develop within them. Version 5.2.0 updates presentation and documentation only. Figure 1 presents the relationship between Big Five representation and Elo alongside the four primary ordinal-model estimates. Figure 2 displays the held-out difference in ignorance score between the joint Big Five + Elo model and Elo alone for each World Cup edition, together with the equal-edition mean and its 95% BCa interval. The former supplementary interval figure was removed; its underlying estimates remain available in the deposited machine-readable results. No data, frozen definition, model specification, inferential estimate, predictive score, random seed or substantive conclusion changed from v5.1.0. The estimand is knockout progression conditional on qualification for the knockout stage. These observational data do not identify a causal effect of Big Five employment, estimate the long-term developmental return to elite-league exposure or address group-stage qualification. The compendium includes analytical data, provenance records, analysis code, machine-readable results and publication-ready figures. The derivative dataset is distributed under CC BY-SA 4.0, with attribution to the Fjelstul World Cup Database.
items.title: Big Five representation, Elo and FIFA World Cup knockout progression, 1998–2026: audited data and reproducibility materials

items.summary: Open-Source Moon: A Technical Framework for Intelligent Development of Extraterrestrial Bodies Based on Sensor Dispersal and Golden Consensus Abstract: The exploration and development of the Moon and other celestial bodies currently depend heavily on State-led, integrated space missions that are costly, slow, and difficult for the public to join. To address this situation, this paper proposes “Open-Source Moon”, a technical framework that applies the open-source philosophy to the intelligent development of extraterrestrial bodies. The framework treats the Moon as a large developer platform that all of humankind can program collectively. Following the progressive principle of “information first, from the outside in, from sensing to action”, it transforms the Moon layer by layer into a “smart planet” that can be programmed as a whole, and it organizes global participation through open-source protocols and the contribution-securing mechanism of “Golden Consensus”: massive numbers of low-cost, standardized micro sensors are first dispersed over the lunar surface to form a distributed sensing network whose nodes are beacons and hotspots; delay-tolerant networking (DTN) and a predictive compensation mechanism then overcome the one-way communication delay of about 1.28 s; and a small-machine cooperation ecosystem, LEGO-style combination of medium-sized machines, and finally unmanned factories and lunar computing carry the staged evolution from sensors to a “smart planet”. Based on the self-similar allocation principle and the Schelling focal point, which secure and incentivize decentralized contributions, a “Golden Consensus” system founded on the golden ratio ( φ ≈ 1.618) is proposed: explorers receive 61.8% of the development-rights return (of which a further 2.8% is set aside as a “common allocation” for public facilities), and 38.2% is designated as socially shared. A model with 880 000 cornerstone nodes is set up, in which a distributed ledger establishes ownership of contributions and keeps tamper-proof records. Verifiable engineering models of network coverage, link budget, energy budget, and delay compensation are established, and the compatibility of this approach with the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, as well as the general applicability of extending it to other celestial bodies such as Mercury and Mars, is demonstrated. This study provides a feasible technical route and governance framework for public participation in the development of extraterrestrial bodies. Keywords: Lunar Landing; Human Lunar Landing ; Open-Source Moon; sensor network; smart planet; Golden Consensus; delay-tolerant networking; lunar development; citizen science; Outer Space Treaty; Human Spaceflight 1. Introduction 1.1. Background and Motivation For more than half a century, the exploration of extraterrestrial bodies has taken the form mainly of large, integrated, State-led missions. After Apollo 17 in 1972, crewed spaceflight remained confined to near-Earth orbit for a long time, until Artemis II completed a crewed lunar flyby (without landing) in April 2026 [1]. On 22 February 2024, the Odysseus lander of Intuitive Machines achieved the first soft landing on the Moon by a commercial spacecraft [2], marking the beginning of the era of commercial lunar landings. However, the development and launch cost of a single mission is still on the order of tens of millions to hundreds of millions of US dollars, and most of the failure risk is concentrated in the powered-descent and landing phases. From the soft landing of Chang’e-3 in 2013 to June 2025, there were 14 soft-landing attempts on the lunar surface worldwide (Table 4): six full successes, three partial successes (in which the attitude or mission capability was impaired after landing), and five failures. According to public reports retrieved for this study, no new lunar landing attempt had occurred

items.summary: MELITE is an open-source Python package for the evaluation and selection of supervised classification and regression models using numeric tabular datasets. It supports classification-only, regression-only, and mixed-task workflows. Model evaluation uses task-specific cross-validation strategies and selection criteria: F1-macro for classification and RMSE for regression. Supported models are optimized with Optuna when hyperparameter tuning is applicable. Evaluation results, optimization summaries, and provenance are preserved in task-specific artifacts. Selected models can be fitted on the full dataset, exported, and reused for prediction. The resulting evaluation evidence supports reproducible model comparison but does not establish external predictive generalizability.
items.title: MELITE — Multi-Model Supervised Learning Evaluator

items.summary: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) shows promise in coordinating connected and automated vehicles but offers no safety guarantee. Although Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) can add this guarantee, their optimization problem can become infeasible in practice due to control bounds. Moreover, they often overapproximate vehicle and road geometry, which makes them conservative. This paper proposes the Backup-Horizon CBF (BH-CBF), which evaluates safety along a horizon until all vehicles stop. BH-CBF is recursively feasible under control bounds, and it considers the exact vehicle and road geometry. Based on BH-CBF, we derive a fully decentralized safety filter that only needs a single broadcast of vehicle states and routes per step and stays real-time in dense traffic. We use BH-CBF to safeguard a MARL policy over its life cycle: as a reward during pre-training, as a run-time filter at deployment, and as a filter in the training loop that keeps fine-tuning on unseen maps collision-free. In simulations on real-world maps of a roundabout and an intersection, BH-CBF avoids all collisions of unsafe MARL policies and keeps its safety guarantee at every step. Existing filters either collide, lose the guarantee, or fall back to full braking far more often. In recorded roundabout traffic with 1264 human-driven vehicles over 115 km, our safeguarded policies shorten the median travel time by 14% compared with the human drivers, without any collision.
items.title: Safeguarding Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Connected and Automated Vehicles with Recursively Feasible Control Barrier Functions

items.summary: Abstract Water balance penalties may improve numerical closure while reallocating error among unobserved ‎fluxes. We investigate this compensation and the limits of selecting a penalty for annual flood ‎prediction. Forty-five trained synthetic LSTMs isolate forcing, exchange, and initialization ‎disturbances. Thirty-five matched regional models and five accounting references use 89 quality-quality-‎screened CAMELS-AUS catchments, partitioned into 54 for development, 15 for selector validation, ‎and 20 for confirmation. Under 40% precipitation underestimation, fixed and bounded penalties ‎reduce estimated evapotranspiration below 1% of generating truth in all eight held-out synthetic ‎catchments. A historically selected rule lowers confirmation-normalized annual-maximum error ‎from 2.29 to 2.21, a 3.54% point reduction. The original conditional interval barely excludes zero, ‎and river-region sign randomization gives p = 0.0625. A post hoc 100,000-draw analysis retains a ‎near-zero upper endpoint, with numerical sub-batches still reaching or crossing zero. Direct paired ‎comparisons with simpler alternatives all span zero; the selector does not establish added predictive ‎value. Its seven active catchments occupy only five regions. Recovery of the original final archive ‎verifies the selection lock, completed fit records, and hashes of all 40 real/reference prediction files. ‎These findings support a controlled latent-compensation mechanism and a reproducible limitation ‎of selective regularization, while leaving real-catchment process attribution and robust predictive ‎superiority unresolved. ‎ Keywords: rainfall-runoff modeling; water balance; annual flood maxima; model misspecification; ‎spatial transfer; uncertainty
items.title: Ayad-Kathim-Hussein/Prof.-Dr.-Ayad-K.-H.-Alkhafaji: Why selective mass penalties do not reliably improve annual flood maxima: An 89-‎catchment diagnostic with recovered provenance

items.summary: This archive contains the Python code, raw numerical results and figure-generation scripts accompanying the paper "An Alternated Inertial Method for Bilevel Split Variational Inequalities Beyond Monotonicity and Lipschitz Continuity" by N. T. T. Thuy and P. T. Hieu (submitted to Optimization, Taylor & Francis, 2026). The paper studies the bilevel split variational inequality problem with multiple output sets (BSVIP-MOS) governed by non-monotone, possibly non-Lipschitz operators, and proposes AISE-VS, an alternated inertial subgradient-extragradient method with a look-ahead self-adaptive stepsize, a split correction and a viscosity step, together with an Armijo line-search variant (AISE-VS-LS) that dispenses with the stepsize conditions. The archive reproduces every table and figure of the paper: - numerical certification of the assumptions (Table 1); - Experiment 1: a certified non-quasimonotone benchmark with skew-type operators, 20 starting points (Table 2, Fig. 1); - Experiment 2: a Hölder (non-Lipschitz) benchmark, self-adaptive rule versus line search, up to 2×10^5 iterations (Table 3, Fig. 2); - Experiment 3: a trade-network instance built from BACI-VI-Bench (year 2022 and a study over 2017–2024) with an independently certified reference solution (Table 4, Fig. 3); - long-run convergence (Fig. 4) and a look-ahead ablation (Fig. 5). The package contains the source code (src/), the raw results behind all tables and figures (results/), the figures (figures/), a README.md that maps each table and figure to the command that regenerates it, run_quick.sh (smoke test) and run_all.sh (full reproduction). Seeds are fixed (global seed 2024). Requirements: Python 3, numpy, scipy, matplotlib. The BACI-VI-Bench dataset (doi:10.5281/zenodo.20607238), derived from CEPII-BACI, is NOT redistributed here; it must be downloaded separately to rerun Experiment 3 (see README). Experiments 1 and 2 are fully synthetic. Version 1.0.1. This version adds the scripts (verification/, run by run_verification.sh) and logs (results/verification/) of the additional checks reported in the revised manuscript. The source code in src/ and all tables and figures are unchanged from version 1.0.0. The checks are: (i) an independent recomputation of the reference solution x† for 2017–2024 with an interior-point solver (CVXPY/Clarabel), compared with the stored x†; (ii) the marginal residual of the stored x†; (iii) an a-posteriori check that every point at which the operators are evaluated stays in the region where the extended operator coincides with the original one; and  (iv) the number of times the restart criterion is examined and the number of times it is activated in Experiments 1–3, including two runs of 10^5 iterations. The logs of one complete run are summarised in results/verification/SUMMARY.md; the version history is in CHANGELOG.md.  Check (i) additionally requires cvxpy (requirements-verification.txt); the other checks need only the packages of requirements.txt.
items.title: AISE-VS for bilevel split variational inequalities with multiple output sets: code and raw results

items.summary: This dataset contains the raw and processed experimental data associated with the study "Eco-Friendly and Large-Scale Fabrication of Microelectronic Silk-Based Enzymatic Biosensors". The collection includes measurements related to silk fibroin film fabrication and characterization, electron-beam lithography process optimization, nanostructure dimensional analysis, and enzymatic activity assays of horseradish peroxidase immobilized within silk fibroin matrices. Raw instrument outputs, processed datasets, statistical analyses, and metadata describing experimental conditions are provided to ensure transparency and reproducibility. The dataset supports the development of environmentally friendly microfabrication strategies for enzyme-based bioelectronic devices and may be reused for studies involving silk fibroin processing, enzyme immobilization, biopolymer lithography, and microelectronic biosensor fabrication
items.title: Replication Data for Eco-Friendly and Large-Scale Fabrication of Microelectronic Silk-Based Enzymatic Biosensors

items.summary: RaMa-Scene Explorer traces the supply chains behind consumption using EXIOBASE v3.3.sm data for 2011. It maps where greenhouse-gas emissions, employment and metal-ore extraction occur across 49 countries and regions, grouped into 15 industry sections. Readers can trace a footprint, inspect its flows and compare 155 published scenarios. Custom scenarios compute on the reader's device, in WebAssembly, or through an optional RaMa-Scene job API. The model changes monetary final demand or inputs per unit of output, with prices and other coefficients fixed. The results describe the 2011 economy, not forecasts. Methods, assumptions, provenance and numerical checks accompany the results. The code is MIT-licensed; derived EXIOBASE data is shared under CC BY 4.0.
items.title: RaMa-Scene Explorer

items.summary: This repository provides the research data, model outputs, analysis scripts, and supporting materials associated with the study “Beyond Architecture: Optimization and Hydrologic Regime Reveal Performance Headroom in Deep-Learning Rainfall–Runoff Modelling.” The study investigates how hyperparameter optimization, hydrological regime information, and ensemble design influence the predictive performance of deep-learning rainfall–runoff models across 531 CAMELS-US catchments. The repository supports the evaluation of regional modelling strategies, hydrologically informed ensembles, configuration-level contributions, and sensitivity analyses. Contents of this release Original research materials: Ten files retained from earlier versions of the dataset, including model archives, predictions, metrics, catchment attributes, and supporting data. 2026 revision analyses: CAMELS_US_Revision_2026_Analysis_Data_v3_additions.zip , containing the additional analysis materials and results underlying the current study, including Top-10 and hydrologically informed ensemble diagnostics, Top-18 sensitivity comparisons, and supporting figure and table resources. Additional Top-18 experiments: CAMELS_US_Top18_Additional8_Raw_10Seed_v3.zip , containing the archived outputs and supporting experiment artifacts for eight additional model configurations evaluated over ten random seeds (80 runs). Version and provenance note This is version 3 of the CAMELS-US research deposit. The files inherited from earlier dataset releases are retained unchanged for provenance and continuity, while the two additional archives document the analyses and experiments introduced in the 2026 release. The version history of the deposit is maintained through Zenodo.
items.title: Beyond Architecture: Optimization and Hydrologic Regime Reveal Performance Headroom in Deep-Learning Rainfall–Runoff Modelling

items.summary: Effective pandemic preparedness depends on the ability to identify, access and reuse health data across borders rapidly. This requires knowing what data and capabilities exist, how infrastructures are governed, which standards they use, and under what conditions data can be accessed or analysed. This work is central to the BE READY European Partnership for Pandemic Preparedness, which aims to strengthen Europe's capacity to coordinate research and respond to emerging infectious disease threats. Comparable, machine-actionable implementation metadata can help BE READY connect existing infrastructures, identify interoperability and governance barriers, and guide strategic investment. This presentation was delivered at the Research Data Alliance (RDA) Plenary 27, hosted by UK Research and Innovation (UKRI), under the theme "Shaping a global open research commons." It examines how fragmented health data infrastructures can become part of a connected, interoperable and sustainable global research ecosystem. The presentation reports two outputs from the RDA Health Data Commons GORC Profile Working Group. The first is the pilot of an implementation metadata survey and profile, building on the RDA Global Open Research Commons (GORC) International Model and FAIR, CARE and TRUST principles. The profile captures technical, legal, governance and equity characteristics of health data commons. Two national biomedical data infrastructures had piloted the survey. The second output is a scoping review of 47 health data infrastructures across 26 countries, described in 74 publications. The review identifies significant reporting gaps in the characteristics needed for interoperability and reuse. Metadata standards were reported for nine infrastructures, APIs for six, identifiers and provenance for two each, and machine-actionable permissions for none. Seven infrastructures supported federated analysis, while three described federated governance. Twenty-one reported legal or governance barriers. Only three described benefit-sharing arrangements, and none reported benefits returned to patients or communities. Just 10 papers reported empirical evidence. These findings reflect gaps in published reporting, which may differ from actual implementation. The RDA Working Group proposes refinements to the GORC International Model covering omics and bioimaging provenance, federated data reuse, and benefit sharing. It also proposes publishing implementation metadata as a living, queryable knowledge graph, supported by a community of practice among health data commons operators. For BE READY, this approach provides a foundation for understanding which European health data capabilities can be mobilised together during a health emergency, what barriers prevent their reuse, and where investment is most needed. More broadly, this work contributes to the RDA P27 ambition of shaping a global open research commons by transforming fragmented infrastructures into a connected, discoverable and interoperable ecosystem that supports research, pandemic preparedness and public health.
items.title: Federated Reuse of Participant-Level Data across Health Data Commons: Evidence, Insights, & Future Directions

items.summary: Real-world geospatial decision support requires more than single-step retrieval or code generation. Disaster-response questions often involve multi-source workflows that combine spatial databases, map-derived features, satellite imagery, raster products, and reusable geospatial artifacts, where correctness depends on preserving spatial scope, temporal context, and intermediate execution state. While large language models and coding agents offer a promising interface for such workflows, they struggle with geospatial-specific failure modes, including handling large artifacts, selecting the wrong evidence source, losing spatial or temporal metadata, and applying invalid geometric operations. We introduce GeoFaham, a domain-specialized multi-agent system for geospatial disaster analytics. GeoFaham decomposes workflows into specialist agents for vector operations, map feature retrieval, imagery discovery, and raster analysis, coordinated by an Orchestrator with a dual-ledger control loop for dependency-aware planning, progress tracking, validation, and replanning. To support artifact-centric collaboration, GeoFaham uses a Response Store that persists full geospatial outputs and typed metadata outside the LLM context window while agents exchange compact identifiers and summaries. We also introduce GeoFaham-Bench, a 40-task benchmark grounded in 17 real-world disaster records, designed to evaluate multi-step geospatial reasoning, cross-source integration, raster-vector computation, artifact generation, and recovery under non-rigid ground truth. We evaluate GeoFaham on GeoFaham-Bench against strong general-purpose coding-agent baselines, including Codex, Claude Code, and OpenCode. GeoFaham achieves the best overall performance, scoring 0.940 versus the next-best 0.879, while using 7.5 times fewer tokens. Our code and benchmark are publicly available at https://github.com/microsoft/GeoFaham.
items.title: GeoFaham: Domain-Specialized Multi-Agent Geospatial Analytics for Disaster Response

items.summary: This package reproduces all tables and figures of the article “Completing Ecosystem Knowledge Graphs: Few-Shot Learning with Calibrated Rules and the Governance of Innovative Start-ups”. The article builds LUCE-KG, an ontology-rich knowledge graph of 15,493 Italian innovative start-ups and SMEs and 25,982 persons. It proposes CRML, a few-shot learner whose predictions are explained by rules with empirical-Bayes calibrated confidences, and tests it on four graphs (FB15k-237, CoDEx-M, NELL-One and LUCE-KG). It then analyses 11,764 firm-years with panel estimators, clustering and explained machine-learning models. Contents code/ : the full pipeline, from graph construction through few-shot completion, baselines (MetaR, TransE, AnyBURL, LLM re-ranking), econometrics, clustering and machine learning, to the build of the manuscript; config/ : few-shot splits, fold assignments, selected hyperparameters and the LUCE-KG ontology; results/ : aggregated results from which every table is built; data_open/ : open-data extracts of the Italian register of innovative start-ups and SMEs (July 2026); README.md with the order of execution, and requirements.txt with software versions. Data not included. Officer and financial records from AIDA (Bureau van Dijk) are licensed and contain personal data, so they are not redistributed. Licensed users can rebuild every input with the scripts provided. The public benchmarks are available from their original sources. Environment. CPU only (2 cores, 8 GB RAM), Python 3.13; the full pipeline takes about 40 CPU-hours. Funding. Project “LUtech Campus Ecosystem—LUCE” (Project Code 22ROJB5), Puglia Region, Program Agreement (Contratto di Programma).
items.title: Replication package for "Completing Ecosystem Knowledge Graphs: Few-Shot Learning with Calibrated Rules and the Governance of Innovative Start-ups"

items.summary: This article connects demographic renewal with multinational recruitment control and the operating life of committed capital. Its host-choice argument engages resource bundling and global staffing, with explicit conditions for shared recruitment, competition and border disruption. Version 3.65.0 adds a Bayesian decision analysis to the Nitra–Puebla staffing appraisal. Under the existing flat-margin, equal-offer-odds benchmark, choosing Nitra after losing the whole UK route carries an expected loss from choosing the wrong host of EUR0.14–1.00 million. Losing only intakes after year fourteen reduces that expected loss to about EUR2,000–15,000. Nitra retains the higher expected value in these reference comparisons. Appendix K11 derives the decision rule, reports alternative priors and provides two independent integrations of 312 specifications. These are conditional public-information appraisals before capital commitment, not realised JLR losses or evidence about its internal contracts. Existing Bayesian panel estimates, demographic inputs, propositions and eight figures are retained. The article distinguishes the measured population-access specification from the recruitment-control mechanism and explains common tenure through the timing of workforce replacement. No observations or regressions are added. Start with Main_Manuscript_ANONYMOUS.pdf, Online_Appendix_ANONYMOUS.pdf and README.txt. Compilable sources, public inputs, code, figure files and aggregate outputs are supplied. The current replication overlay and nine frozen base archives restore the complete permitted replication. Licensed WRDS rows require subscriber access; queries and reconstruction instructions are supplied. Editor-only cover and title pages are excluded.
items.title: Borrowed Youth: Demographic Change and Multinational Location Advantage — Article and Replication Materials

items.summary: Long-horizon multi-agent systems suffer from three tightly coupled failures: task drift, role drift, and state staleness. We test the hypothesis that these share a common representational cause: agent hidden states move away from the directions encoding the active task, assigned role, and current shared state. A pilot study over 14,832 annotated turns supports this: drifted turns collapse near-uniformly across all three anchor subspaces (pairwise r = 0.72-0.78). Existing methods address these failures separately, operating at the surface-text level or treating control directions independently. We introduce ATLAS (Algebraic Task-role Locking with Adaptive Spectral Memory), a training-free intervention acting on hidden states before a token is generated. ATLAS builds a positive-semidefinite anchor kernel over task, role, and state subspaces and steers hidden states toward their shared high-coherence eigendirections; a low-rank Gram decomposition keeps this tractable. Across long-horizon memory, state maintenance, tool use, least-privilege coordination, and embodied stress tests, ATLAS outperforms prompting, retrieval, memory, and activation-steering baselines. Against A-MEM it improves memory macro-average accuracy by up to 5.7 points and reduces write/read failures by up to 31.7%/24.8%; against MemoryArena-Agent it gains up to 4.8 points. It gains 10.7-12.1 points under perturbation, reaches 93.5% role consistency, and transfers to a 72B backbone (macro-average 61.0 vs. 56.2). Ablating the joint task-role-state span costs 7.2 points against 0.8 for a matched-rank random span, indicating these directions are functionally implicated, not incidental; supplying them by prompt or retrieval recovers 4.3 points less. ATLAS is therefore a representation-level controller for open-weight multi-agent systems, complementary to output-level protocols for black-box agents.
items.title: Drift No More: Spectral Locking for Long-Horizon Open-Weight Multi-Agent AI

Historical starter status derives from the Fjelstul World Cup Database and was cross-checked against RSSSF match details. Club affiliation and top-division status were adjudicated using tournament squad records and season-specific domestic-league reference files. The 2014–2026 subset retains the completed provenance audit, including 505 re-checked starter records, 13 starter-name corrections, 45 club-affiliation checks and seven Big Five reclassifications. Analyses include tournament-adjusted ordinal and cut-point models, AICc comparison with Akaike weights, 5,000 national-team cluster-bootstrap samples with bias-corrected and accelerated intervals, leave-one-edition-out validation, leave-one-national-team-out validation, a strict 2026 temporal and tournament-format holdout, and a predictive cluster bootstrap that refits both competing models within every fold and resample. Additional checks address collinearity, edition adjustment and dependence through within-edition permutation testing and an edition-level block bootstrap. Big Five representation was associated with deeper knockout progression before adjustment for Elo, but this association attenuated after adjustment. Model comparisons and held-out evaluations did not establish a stable, transportable increment beyond prior team strength. These findings concern the predictive information provided by current league representation; they do not distinguish the mechanisms through which players enter elite leagues or develop within them. Version 5.2.0 updates presentation and documentation only. Figure 1 presents the relationship between Big Five representation and Elo alongside the four primary ordinal-model estimates. Figure 2 displays the held-out difference in ignorance score between the joint Big Five + Elo model and Elo alone for each World Cup edition, together with the equal-edition mean and its 95% BCa interval. The former supplementary interval figure was removed; its underlying estimates remain available in the deposited machine-readable results. No data, frozen definition, model specification, inferential estimate, predictive score, random seed or substantive conclusion changed from v5.1.0. The estimand is knockout progression conditional on qualification for the knockout stage. These observational data do not identify a causal effect of Big Five employment, estimate the long-term developmental return to elite-league exposure or address group-stage qualification. The compendium includes analytical data, provenance records, analysis code, machine-readable results and publication-ready figures. The derivative dataset is distributed under CC BY-SA 4.0, with attribution to the Fjelstul World Cup Database.
items.title: Big Five representation, Elo and FIFA World Cup knockout progression, 1998–2026: audited data and reproducibility materials

items.summary: This archive contains the Python code, raw numerical results and figure-generation scripts accompanying the paper "An Alternated Inertial Method for Bilevel Split Variational Inequalities Beyond Monotonicity and Lipschitz Continuity" by N. T. T. Thuy and P. T. Hieu (submitted to Optimization, Taylor & Francis, 2026). The paper studies the bilevel split variational inequality problem with multiple output sets (BSVIP-MOS) governed by non-monotone, possibly non-Lipschitz operators, and proposes AISE-VS, an alternated inertial subgradient-extragradient method with a look-ahead self-adaptive stepsize, a split correction and a viscosity step, together with an Armijo line-search variant (AISE-VS-LS) that dispenses with the stepsize conditions. The archive reproduces every table and figure of the paper: - numerical certification of the assumptions (Table 1); - Experiment 1: a certified non-quasimonotone benchmark with skew-type operators, 20 starting points (Table 2, Fig. 1); - Experiment 2: a Hölder (non-Lipschitz) benchmark, self-adaptive rule versus line search, up to 2×10^5 iterations (Table 3, Fig. 2); - Experiment 3: a trade-network instance built from BACI-VI-Bench (year 2022 and a study over 2017–2024) with an independently certified reference solution (Table 4, Fig. 3); - long-run convergence (Fig. 4) and a look-ahead ablation (Fig. 5). The package contains the source code (src/), the raw results behind all tables and figures (results/), the figures (figures/), a README.md that maps each table and figure to the command that regenerates it, run_quick.sh (smoke test) and run_all.sh (full reproduction). Seeds are fixed (global seed 2024). Requirements: Python 3, numpy, scipy, matplotlib. The BACI-VI-Bench dataset (doi:10.5281/zenodo.20607238), derived from CEPII-BACI, is NOT redistributed here; it must be downloaded separately to rerun Experiment 3 (see README). Experiments 1 and 2 are fully synthetic. Version 1.0.1. This version adds the scripts (verification/, run by run_verification.sh) and logs (results/verification/) of the additional checks reported in the revised manuscript. The source code in src/ and all tables and figures are unchanged from version 1.0.0. The checks are: (i) an independent recomputation of the reference solution x† for 2017–2024 with an interior-point solver (CVXPY/Clarabel), compared with the stored x†; (ii) the marginal residual of the stored x†; (iii) an a-posteriori check that every point at which the operators are evaluated stays in the region where the extended operator coincides with the original one; and  (iv) the number of times the restart criterion is examined and the number of times it is activated in Experiments 1–3, including two runs of 10^5 iterations. The logs of one complete run are summarised in results/verification/SUMMARY.md; the version history is in CHANGELOG.md.  Check (i) additionally requires cvxpy (requirements-verification.txt); the other checks need only the packages of requirements.txt.
items.title: AISE-VS for bilevel split variational inequalities with multiple output sets: code and raw results

items.summary: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) shows promise in coordinating connected and automated vehicles but offers no safety guarantee. Although Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) can add this guarantee, their optimization problem can become infeasible in practice due to control bounds. Moreover, they often overapproximate vehicle and road geometry, which makes them conservative. This paper proposes the Backup-Horizon CBF (BH-CBF), which evaluates safety along a horizon until all vehicles stop. BH-CBF is recursively feasible under control bounds, and it considers the exact vehicle and road geometry. Based on BH-CBF, we derive a fully decentralized safety filter that only needs a single broadcast of vehicle states and routes per step and stays real-time in dense traffic. We use BH-CBF to safeguard a MARL policy over its life cycle: as a reward during pre-training, as a run-time filter at deployment, and as a filter in the training loop that keeps fine-tuning on unseen maps collision-free. In simulations on real-world maps of a roundabout and an intersection, BH-CBF avoids all collisions of unsafe MARL policies and keeps its safety guarantee at every step. Existing filters either collide, lose the guarantee, or fall back to full braking far more often. In recorded roundabout traffic with 1264 human-driven vehicles over 115 km, our safeguarded policies shorten the median travel time by 14% compared with the human drivers, without any collision.
items.title: Safeguarding Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Connected and Automated Vehicles with Recursively Feasible Control Barrier Functions

items.summary: Fractal Geometry and the Verifiability of Electronic Election Results: Limits of Identification and a Multiscale Framework for Analyzing Tabulation This record contains an integrated research article (preprint; not peer reviewed) that asks a deliberately narrow question: under what conditions can fractal and multiscale methods applied to the published tabulation of a two-candidate election yield useful statistical evidence of irregularity, and under what conditions can no such method identify the origin of the data? The paper is addressed equally to those who read smoothness in a tabulation curve as a certificate of integrity and to those who read any irregularity as proof of manipulation; it argues that both readings mistake arithmetic and model specification for evidence. The analysis separates five stages of the electoral chain (voter choice, machine record, transmission, tabulation, publication) and three research questions that are routinely conflated: whether the order in which precincts are reported is atypical, whether precinct-level results are atypical relative to an explicit reference model, and whether published results agree with independently preserved records. Three elementary propositions formalize what tabulation data can and cannot show. The cumulative vote share is mechanically damped as the count grows, so late smoothness is a property of weighted averaging rather than a sign of control. Two scenarios that induce the same distribution over the observable data cannot be separated by any test confined to those data, with discriminating power bounded by their total variation distance. And a class of proportional vote transfers leaves every increment-based statistic (first differences, centered CUSUM, zero-mean wavelet contrasts) unchanged while shifting the cumulative margin by 2δN_k. A fully synthetic experiment models 256 precincts in 16 regions with correlated regional preferences and geographically dependent reporting times, and compares four two-sided detectors (level test, centered CUSUM, multiscale scan and Haar contrast over windows of 4 to 128 precincts), each calibrated separately on 2,000 null elections and evaluated on 1,500 independent elections per scenario. Under the correct null, alert rates lie between 4.1% and 5.7%. With a 4% transfer concentrated in a block of 51 precincts, the Haar contrast alerts in 94.0% of replicates (Wilson 95% interval 92.7%–95.1%); with a diffuse 0.8% transfer across all 256 precincts, moving approximately the same number of votes (608 versus 612 on average), it alerts in 4.5%, indistinguishable from the null. A legitimate regional preference shift omitted from the reference model produces Haar alerts in 57.7% of elections in which no vote was transferred, and a deliberately homogeneous reference that ignores geography drives three of the four detectors to 100% false alerts. Sensitivity depends on the shape of the alteration and on the specification of the reference model, not on the volume of votes moved. The limits of these findings are stated explicitly. The reference model is an oracle known to the simulator; all data are synthetic; the experiment was not preregistered; detection delay and localization accuracy were not systematically evaluated; no actual election is analyzed, and nothing in the paper certifies or refutes the integrity of any election. A p-value is not a probability of fraud, and the absence of an alert cannot certify the absence of manipulation. The paper closes with a protocol for future application to real tabulation records, covering data provenance and chronology, preregistration, a global multiscale statistic with Monte Carlo calibration, nonfractal comparators at equal false-alert rates, adversarial and benign alternatives, and robustness checks, and situates the discussion within software independence and the cast-as-intended, recorded-as-cast and tallied-as-recorded framework of election verifiability. items.summary: In LLM-based recommendation, memory acts as a user-level agent in a memory-augmented backbone. Yet users and items remain asymmetric: only the user is given a structured profile; it enters a bandwidth-limited reranker prompt; and it is frozen after warmup. We recast LLM-based recommendation as an agentic-communication process in four stages: BUILD a self-description, TRANSMIT it along the collaborative graph, UNDERSTAND the other side, and SYNC it from the next interaction. This formulation reveals three unresolved communication challenges: the item side never produces a comparable self-description (one-sided BUILD); profile-level signals enter only the bandwidth-limited reranker prompt rather than retrieval, where they would not compete for context tokens (prompt-trapped UNDERSTAND); and the user's description is frozen after warmup with no principled update rule (absent SYNC). We instantiate the missing stages as HARP (Homophily-aware Agentic Recommendation via dual Profiles), a training-free, three-operator addition to a frozen LLM backbone: a rule-extracted symmetric item profile (zero extra LLM calls), a channel-decomposable profile-level homophily H(phi_u, phi_i) consumed at retrieval time rather than inside the reranker prompt, and a single-pass reflective update realising in-context profile evolution without any gradient step. On four public benchmarks (Yelp, Books, MovieTV, Goodreads), HARP lifts Hit@1 over the strongest published baseline by 6.9%-24.0%, with family-wise Holm-corrected p < 1e-9 on every dataset. Ablations and a per-case attribution study show that the operators contribute complementary gains, with the retrieval-side gate as the main source; we also report the trade-off introduced by the reflective pass. We formulate agentic communication and provide a training-free instantiation. Code is available at https://github.com/Jove-Zhen/HARP.
items.title: HARP: Training-Free Dual-Profile Agentic Communication for LLM-Based Recommendation

items.summary: Code, derived data and result files for Differentiable Neuro-Fuzzy Reasoning (DNFR), a path-based link predictor that learns degree-aware edge memberships, a Schweizer–Sklar t-norm per metapath and metapath reliabilities, and aggregates paths by noisy-OR, used as an instrument for a controlled component analysis on medical knowledge graphs. Tasks: drug repurposing in Hetionet v1.0 and PrimeKG, disease–symptom prediction in Hetionet and in the graded health knowledge graph of Rotmensch et al. (2017), and a secondary test on a NHANES fuzzy relation, under leave-dyad-out random and disease-centred splits. Comparators: fixed t-norms, component ablations, restarts of the t-norm parameter, DWPC with logistic regression (with and without degree and prior features), a degree-preserving edge prior, popularity, AnyBURL, truncated and soft-thresholded SVD and knowledge graph embeddings. Version v3.0-rev3 (third revision) adds DNFR 2.0, four refinements tested one at a time and in combination (overlap-aware aggregation, Gumbel-softmax operator choice, an information-content hub discount and membership annealing), a fixed t-norm selected on validation data, a converged L-BFGS profile of the t-norm parameter, an unbounded parameterisation, a compact NBFNet baseline, an exact edge-level Shapley attribution of the explanations, a mechanistic classification of the drug-repurposing explanations, a sparsity variant that keeps the target relation, and 10 leave-dyad-out splits for the main comparisons on Hetionet compound–treats–disease, Hetionet disease–symptom and the graded health knowledge graph. Version 1.1.0 (second revision) added a profile analysis of the t-norm parameter, training without early stopping, additional splits, equivalence tests, the edge prior, share-matched and edge-level explanation tests, unit tests and the script that builds the manuscript from the statistics files. Includes per-query ranks for every method and split, trained models, path explanations, and the statistics files from which every number in the manuscript is read. Hetionet and PrimeKG are downloaded by download_data.py with MD5 checks.
items.title: Code and derived results for: Which parts of a neuro-fuzzy path reasoner should be learned? A controlled component analysis on medical knowledge graphs, with four refinements (DNFR 2.0)

items.summary: This dataset contains the raw and processed experimental data associated with the study "Eco-Friendly and Large-Scale Fabrication of Microelectronic Silk-Based Enzymatic Biosensors". The collection includes measurements related to silk fibroin film fabrication and characterization, electron-beam lithography process optimization, nanostructure dimensional analysis, and enzymatic activity assays of horseradish peroxidase immobilized within silk fibroin matrices. Raw instrument outputs, processed datasets, statistical analyses, and metadata describing experimental conditions are provided to ensure transparency and reproducibility. The dataset supports the development of environmentally friendly microfabrication strategies for enzyme-based bioelectronic devices and may be reused for studies involving silk fibroin processing, enzyme immobilization, biopolymer lithography, and microelectronic biosensor fabrication
items.title: Replication Data for Eco-Friendly and Large-Scale Fabrication of Microelectronic Silk-Based Enzymatic Biosensors

items.summary: MELITE is an open-source Python package for the evaluation and selection of supervised classification and regression models using numeric tabular datasets. It supports classification-only, regression-only, and mixed-task workflows. Model evaluation uses task-specific cross-validation strategies and selection criteria: F1-macro for classification and RMSE for regression. Supported models are optimized with Optuna when hyperparameter tuning is applicable. Evaluation results, optimization summaries, and provenance are preserved in task-specific artifacts. Selected models can be fitted on the full dataset, exported, and reused for prediction. The resulting evaluation evidence supports reproducible model comparison but does not establish external predictive generalizability.
items.title: MELITE — Multi-Model Supervised Learning Evaluator

items.summary: Split Inference (SI) addresses the hardware resource limitations of Internet of Things (IoT) devices by distributing tiny Machine Learning (TinyML) model segments across multiple IoT devices. However, a device failure can interrupt the inference pipeline. This paper proposes a replica-aware recovery approach that deploys replicas of TinyML model segments originally hosted on failed devices onto surviving devices. We formulate the joint selection of replica hosts and communication protocols as a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) problem that minimizes post-reconfiguration inference latency, accounting for computation and transmission latencies, under flash memory and runtime memory constraints. Simulations using MobileNetV2 on heterogeneous IoT networks compare the proposed approach with four baselines. We implement the model in a network of 15 IoT devices with a maximum link-rate reduction of 75%, and show that MILP approach achieves an average modeled end-to-end inference latency that is 6.8% lower than that of Computation Greedy and 18.3% lower than that of Random. Index Terms TinyML, split inference, Internet of Things, fault tolerance, replica placement.
items.title: Replica-Aware Split Inference for Edge IoT Systems

items.summary: This record contains the Python code and the reference outputs for the manuscript *How much can a bonus–malus scale learn? Finite memory and the design of experience rating* by Wei Zhu (University of Groningen).   The code treats a bonus–malus system as a finite-state estimator of a policyholder's claim propensity, evaluated by Norberg's credibility criterion. It computes the share of the variance of the claim propensity explained by no-claim discounts, −1/+m scales and hidden-counter scales as the number of classes grows; benchmarks for any rule with a given number of memory states (optimisation over tilted binomial and multinomial laws, exhaustive and heuristic search over deterministic machines, the van Trees lower bound); the evaluation of fourteen historical bonus–malus scales in the long run, at finite policy ages and with one premium scale for all ages; out-of-sample tests and a segmented-tariff analysis on a public French motor panel (1999–2007); and checks against the published tables of Norberg (1976) and Borgan, Hoem and Norberg (1981).   README.md maps every table and result of the paper to the script that produces it. The French motor data (CASdatasets, fremotor2/3/4freq9907b) are public and are not included; data/README.md lists the files and their SHA-256 checksums. Requirements: Python 3.11 or later with NumPy, SciPy, pandas, Matplotlib, mpmath, rdata and xarray.   Version 1.1.0 accompanies the version of the manuscript submitted to the Annals of Actuarial Science: flat layout (code/, results/), three scripts added for the revised manuscript (brier_translation.py, design_levers.py, det_exhaustive_reducible.py), a replication script run_all.py, and a README mapped to the current numbering of tables, sections and propositions. The computations of the scripts in version 1.0.0 are unchanged.
items.title: Code for: How much can a bonus-malus scale learn? Finite memory and the design of experience rating

items.summary: Saigon300 is a semi-synthetic benchmark for the Vehicle Routing Problem with Time Windows (VRPTW) in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam. Version 1.0.0 archives 56 instances with 300 customers and one depot each: C1 (9), C2 (8), R1 (12), R2 (11), RC1 (8), and RC2 (8). The package contains eight shared asymmetric OSRM distance/duration matrices, instance files, BIH verification and OR-Tools code, figures, and recorded experimental outputs. Matrix units are metres and seconds; the routing profile is car. Source metadata reports an OpenStreetMap snapshot dated 2026-05-26. This deposit is an unchanged snapshot of public repository commit 555ac7d2eb9d2af402bdb23f9633e3af435d8ab4: https://github.com/ltlong-SGU/Saigon300-VRPTW . ZIP integrity and node IDs 0..300 for all 56 instance files have been checked. This is not a new solver experiment or full independent replication. Authors: Le Tan Long and Phan Tan Quoc (Saigon University); Do Phan Thuan (Ho Chi Minh City University of Industry and Trade), as stated in the source metadata. Original source licences are retained: CC BY 4.0 for the dataset; source metadata separately declares MIT for code. Upstream rights remain applicable to OpenStreetMap/OSRM-derived components; OpenStreetMap attribution: https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright . This dataset deposit is separate from the accepted Saigon300 camera-ready paper, which is not included.
items.title: Saigon300: A VRPTW Benchmark Dataset for Urban Delivery in Ho Chi Minh City

items.summary: What are the capacity limits of a bounded observer’s epistemic activity, and what constructions attain those limits? This technical and philosophical companion connects preservation, acquisition and discovery, construction, certification, adoption, continuation and revision, with resource accounting, self-application and coverage throughout. The full connected capacity characterization remains OPEN. Interim technical revision r7t, 4 November 2026. This corrected successor improves the reader’s guide, lifecycle explanation, prior-work comparisons and model-to-system discussion. It preserves the published finite-Fourier orbit-separating construction with its explicit nonzero-reference condition, arithmetic-cost model and conditioning limits. Orientation is an explanatory atlas, not a proof premise. Exact results, assumptions and review evidence govern mathematical claims. The revision qualifies empirical-verification and identifiability statements by their evidence models; separates expected, probabilistic and worst-case guarantees; and distinguishes imported mathematics from unresolved transfer obligations. Historical cases and dated internal AI-agent trials illustrate the lens without establishing universal performance or research novelty. It separates native builder controls from generated-application behavior, passing local checks from authorized outcomes, and prospective tests from completed observations. Review is internal and AI-assisted, not external peer review or whole-program mathematical acceptance. Earlier versions and dated evidence cutoffs are preserved. This is an explanatory and corrective edition, not a claim that the full research program is complete. The manuscript retains its review-candidate designation. This record contains the manuscript, not a standalone proof-reproduction package.
items.title: The Missing Distinction: The Connected Capacity of a Bounded Observer

items.summary: Abstract Water balance penalties may improve numerical closure while reallocating error among unobserved ‎fluxes. We investigate this compensation and the limits of selecting a penalty for annual flood ‎prediction. Forty-five trained synthetic LSTMs isolate forcing, exchange, and initialization ‎disturbances. Thirty-five matched regional models and five accounting references use 89 quality-quality-‎screened CAMELS-AUS catchments, partitioned into 54 for development, 15 for selector validation, ‎and 20 for confirmation. Under 40% precipitation underestimation, fixed and bounded penalties ‎reduce estimated evapotranspiration below 1% of generating truth in all eight held-out synthetic ‎catchments. A historically selected rule lowers confirmation-normalized annual-maximum error ‎from 2.29 to 2.21, a 3.54% point reduction. The original conditional interval barely excludes zero, ‎and river-region sign randomization gives p = 0.0625. A post hoc 100,000-draw analysis retains a ‎near-zero upper endpoint, with numerical sub-batches still reaching or crossing zero. Direct paired ‎comparisons with simpler alternatives all span zero; the selector does not establish added predictive ‎value. Its seven active catchments occupy only five regions. Recovery of the original final archive ‎verifies the selection lock, completed fit records, and hashes of all 40 real/reference prediction files. ‎These findings support a controlled latent-compensation mechanism and a reproducible limitation ‎of selective regularization, while leaving real-catchment process attribution and robust predictive ‎superiority unresolved. ‎ Keywords: rainfall-runoff modeling; water balance; annual flood maxima; model misspecification; ‎spatial transfer; uncertainty
items.title: Ayad-Kathim-Hussein/Prof.-Dr.-Ayad-K.-H.-Alkhafaji: Why selective mass penalties do not reliably improve annual flood maxima: An 89-‎catchment diagnostic with recovered provenance
